APPLICATION GUIDE

Dongfeng KTA1 8x4 Electric Dump Truck for Urban Construction

Evaluate the 31 t GVW KTA1 configuration against the actual construction haul cycle, body, site access, charging and payload calculation.

APPLICATIONSeptember 29, 20269 min read
In this guideKTA1 specificationConstruction cycleBody and payloadEnergy planningSite readinessLimitationsBuyer checklistFAQ

Catalogue-listed KTA1 specification

The project catalogue lists KTA1 as an 8x4 electric dump truck in the 31 t gross vehicle weight class. The same model row shows a 352 kWh battery, 270 kW rated and 450 kW peak motor output, 4AMT transmission, wheelbase segments of 1,995 + 3,600 + 1,350 mm, DF451S / DF440 axle entries, 11.00R20 tyres, EBS + ESC and GB charging. Use this as an initial product-screening view, then require a build-specific technical schedule before comparing offers.

ItemKTA1 catalogue entryWhat the project must confirm
Layout / weight class8x4 / 31 t GVWApproved completed vehicle mass and axle loads
Battery352 kWhExact pack, usable energy guidance and mass
Motor / transmission270 / 450 kW; 4AMTFinal equipment and duty-cycle limits
Wheelbase1,995 + 3,600 + 1,350 mmBody drawings and mounting compatibility
Axles / tyresDF451S / DF440; 11.00R20Axle loads, tyre rating and site surface
Charging / safetyGB; EBS + ESCCharger match and delivered safety equipment

GVW must not be described as payload. Allowable payload depends on the completed truck's curb mass, body and equipment, axle distribution, legal limits and market approval. A dump body can materially affect mass, center of gravity and chassis interfaces. Get the body-builder's design and the chassis supplier's approved mounting information before calculating the tonnes of material per trip.

Map the construction haul cycle step by step

Urban construction work may involve a material source, a city access road, a restricted site, repeated loading and unloading, queues and a return route. Record each leg separately: distance, grade, surface, speed, loaded mass, empty mass, stop duration and expected cycles per shift. Include access ramps, temporary roads, waiting at a gate, tipping location and any detour required by construction traffic. Do not extrapolate from the distance alone; a short steep climb under load may affect energy and time more than a longer level segment.

Identify which tasks are predictable and which depend on the site. A controlled project with stable loading points and return-to-depot charging differs from a truck reassigned among multiple sites each day. Note whether it must pass public roads, low bridges, tight turns or weight-controlled streets. Check the turning circle and the complete combination around loading areas, not only in the depot. The dispatch plan should state who can change the route and how the driver reports an unplanned detour.

For each site, confirm the material, loading method, loading duration, tip method, ground stability and space around the discharge area. The article's general context does not establish suitability for a specific material or body. Obtain the relevant design approvals and safe operating procedures from the body builder, site operator and local authorities.

Choose the body and calculate payload as a completed vehicle

“Dump truck” describes a vocation, not one universal body. Confirm the material density range, volume requirement, tipping direction, tailgate design, liner needs, cover, hydraulic system and duty frequency. A larger volume does not necessarily increase legal payload; light bulk and dense material can load the same body to very different masses. Weigh representative loads and define how loading will be controlled. Include tools, guards, spare wheel, driver, fluids and any optional equipment when determining completed mass.

Coordinate the body interface early. Ask for chassis frame drawings, mounting points, permissible center-of-gravity range, axle load envelope, electrical connection details and the approved power interface for the body equipment. The catalogue entry lists a 4AMT driveline but does not specify every dump-body hydraulic arrangement. Do not assume a body PTO, hydraulic pump or control system is included. Have the chassis and body suppliers agree who is responsible for integration, commissioning and documentation.

For an 8x4 design, the number and placement of axles do not automatically prove that the vehicle will meet every project's ground pressure or turning requirements. Review front and rear axle loads at empty, partial and full body states. Include the approach, tipping and return cycle in the analysis. Ask the supplier to provide the relevant drawings and calculations rather than inferring load distribution from the model label.

Assess 352 kWh against energy per shift

The 352 kWh catalogue capacity does not define how many site cycles the KTA1 can complete. Energy depends on gross mass, payload, elevation, rolling surface, idle time, ambient temperature, cab climate and body operation. Where possible, measure a representative shift using a comparable vehicle or a pilot. Record start and finish SOC, energy drawn, distance, cycles, loaded and empty mass, waiting, tipping and charging supplied. Keep a challenging but normal day in view; a weekly average can hide a shift that fails to finish.

Set a reserve for traffic, access changes, charger unavailability and the energy needed to reach the next safe charging point. Use the approved SOC operating guidance for the exact vehicle. Compare expected energy with the shift and rest schedule. If charging must happen on site, confirm that the equipment and location are compatible with dust, water, impact risk, traffic flow and the site's electrical supply. Arrange cable management and protective separation in consultation with qualified site and electrical professionals.

Don't turn the peak motor output into a guarantee of cycle productivity. It is not a statement of sustained performance on a given grade, nor a substitute for a route and thermal review. Ask for the operating limits that apply to the selected build and get a duty-cycle assessment when grades or continuous high-load work are important.

Check whether the site can support daily operation

Before selecting a truck, review the entire daily path from depot to loading point, along the route and through the tipping area. Identify height restrictions, bridge limits, turning areas, gradients, low traction surfaces, road works and zones where charging or parking is prohibited. Ask the site operator to confirm permitted vehicle dimensions, axle loads and operating hours. In an active construction zone, the route may change; define a safe process for reassessment rather than leaving route decisions informal.

Plan depot readiness as a fleet project. Determine where vehicles park, how chargers are protected from reversing movements, who controls access, whether charging can overlap loading, and how an unavailable charger is escalated. Have an appropriately qualified professional review electrical supply, protection, earthing, cable routing and emergency access for the actual installation. This article does not specify charger capacity or installation design.

Plan people and support too: operator training, charging responsibilities, cleaning around inlets, daily defect checks, maintenance escalation and spare equipment. Construction conditions can be demanding for tyres, brakes, suspension, cooling and body hardware. Agree the inspection routine with the vehicle and body suppliers. Confirm authorized service capability and parts logistics before the first vehicle arrives.

What this catalogue entry cannot tell you

Available data does not establish actual payload, range, trips per shift, charge duration, price, warranty, certification or performance on a particular construction surface. Nor does it guarantee that every option in the model row is currently available for every destination. Those answers require a specific completed-vehicle configuration, test or engineering assessment, and applicable local approval.

Avoid choosing only by battery size or the 450 kW peak figure. The complete task includes the body, material, road, load, cycle time, charging window, site power and service coverage. Avoid comparing a 31 t GVW entry directly with the payload of a competing completed vehicle. Compare like-for-like body, legal limits, operating assumptions and commercial scope.

KTA1 project checklist

  • Destination market, registration use, route permissions and site weight restrictions.
  • Exact completed vehicle mass, axle loads, body, material and payload calculation.
  • Representative loaded and empty route legs, grade, surface, queues and trips per shift.
  • Body drawings, hydraulic/electrical interface, tipping process and approved mounting.
  • Measured or validated energy per shift, operating reserve and charge window.
  • Charging equipment compatibility, site supply, bay layout and outage contingency.
  • Tyres, axle setup, braking, safety equipment and construction-site inspection plan.
  • Driver training, maintenance scope, spare parts, warranty and delivery inclusions.

Use the Dongfeng electric dump-truck range to compare other listed classes, including the separate 55 t TZ3Z entry and heavy TZ models. To request a KTA1 proposal, send the site route, material, body, daily cycle and charger plan.

Frequently asked questions

Is 31 t GVW the KTA1 payload?

No. GVW is the gross vehicle weight entry, not payload. The completed truck mass, body, axle limits and local approval determine allowable payload.

How many construction trips can it complete?

The catalogue does not publish a validated trip count. It must be assessed from route energy, loads, body work, charging and reserve.

Does the catalogue include a dump body?

The model row provides chassis and powertrain details but does not establish the exact body package. Confirm body scope and integration in the signed offer.
